blurbs/formal-methods-ancient-greece.title: Formal Methods in Ancient Greece
blurbs/formal-methods-ancient-greece.content:
A child learning about animals works it out for themselves: all birds fly; a robin is a bird; so robins fly. The rule holds for sparrows, crows, and pigeons, and soon the child can apply it to birds they have never seen. Then, on a trip to the zoo, they meet a penguin. Nothing was wrong with the reasoning; its form was flawless. The trouble was that the rule never looked at what “bird” meant, or at the actual birds it was supposed to describe. It cared only about the shape of the argument.
From the Concrete to the Abstract
By the 4th century BCE, humans, remarkable pattern recognizers that we are, were already leaping from a handful of concrete, living examples to abstract forms that could cover infinitely many cases. Aristotle (384–322 BCE) popularized this move with his codification of syllogisms [@aristotle350prior]. Consider a few examples of how reasoning shifts from the particular to the general:

Concrete inference instance: all mammals give birth to live young; a cat is a mammal; therefore a cat gives birth to live young.
Concrete inference instance: all humans are mortal; Socrates is a human; therefore Socrates is mortal.
Abstract inference rule: all Xs are Y; Z is an X; therefore Z is Y.

This is hardly surprising to anyone familiar with modern logic or computation, yet it reveals a key tension between abstraction and context. In moving from the concrete to the abstract, we gain a rule that applies to any statements matching the same form. But we also begin to value a certain kind of forgetting: disregarding what X, Y, and Z actually stand for. The power of the rule depends on that act of erasure. Over time, this habit of forgetting becomes a programming culture virtue, enabling the cognitive offloading of judgment and decision-making.  Such abstractionism shapes not only mathematics and logic but also the social systems that depend on them.

blurbs/heidegger.title: Heidegger and Software
blurbs/heidegger.content:
You are writing a report that is due in an hour, and it is going well. You are in the flow, typing away, sentences arriving almost as fast as you can get them down, thinking only about what you want to say. Then the cursor stops. A small wheel begins to spin, the keys you press go nowhere, and a window announces that the application is not responding. Just like that, you are torn out of the flow and confronted with everything you had stopped noticing: the keyboard under your fingers, the glowing screen, the toolbar of tiny icons, the file system somewhere underneath. Did it save? When did it last save? Where does the file actually live, and what exactly is a “recovered document”? A minute ago you were writing; now you are wrestling with the machinery of writing.
When Technology Disappears
Technological complexity tends to vanish when it works smoothly and resurface when it fails. Most of the time, our tools blend into the background, letting us focus on the task rather than the mechanism. In Being and Time [-@heidegger1927being], Heidegger described this contrast through his notions of ready-to-hand and present-at-hand. When things function smoothly, we relate to them as ready-to-hand, absorbed in use, not noticed as separate objects. A hammer, for example, disappears into the act of hammering, becoming almost an extension of the body. But when the hammer slips, breaks, or hits the thumb, it suddenly becomes present-at-hand—a thing that demands attention and analysis. This shift, from seamless use to reflective awareness, reveals what Heidegger saw as the basic structure of our engagement with the world: we live first in practical involvement, and only when that flow is interrupted do we step back to see objects as objects. Simondon had a similar conception of how technologies become transparent to the user.
Neuroscience offers a striking parallel. Iriki, Tanaka, and Iwamura [-@iriki1996coding] trained macaque monkeys to retrieve food with a rake while recording from neurons that respond both to touch on the hand and to things seen near it. While the monkeys used the rake, the visual receptive fields of these neurons stretched out along the tool, as if the hand now ended at the rake’s tip. Umiltà and colleagues [-@umilta2008pliers] trained monkeys to grasp with ordinary pliers and with “reverse” pliers, which close when the hand opens. Neurons that fire when a monkey grasps with its hand also fired when it grasped with either tool, and they kept time with the closing of the tool’s jaws, even when that required the opposite movement of the fingers. In both cases the brain seems to absorb the tool into the body and to represent the goal of the action rather than the movement that achieves it, much as Heidegger’s hammer disappears into hammering.
Winograd and Flores later applied this same phenomenological insight to computing in Understanding Computers and Cognition [-@winograd1987understanding]. They noted that early computer interfaces often failed precisely because they disrupted this seamless absorption: crashes, bugs, and rigid command structures pulled users out of their task and made them confront the system’s internal logic. Programmers today describe the same effect as an abstraction leak: a moment when the polished surface of technology cracks and the buried complexity beneath becomes visible. Each glitch or failure is a small phenomenological fracture, a reminder that every smooth interface hides a dense machinery of dependencies waiting to announce itself.

blurbs/llull-leibniz.title: Early Mechanical Reasoning and the Dream of Universal Calculation
blurbs/llull-leibniz.content:
Two people stand before a judge on similar charges. Before sentencing, each has answered a long questionnaire: prior convictions, but also when they first had contact with the police, whether friends or family have records, what kind of neighbourhood they grew up in. A statistical model turns the answers into a recidivism risk score, and that score can weigh on how long each of them spends in prison. Across town, a family applies for a mortgage online; within a minute, a scoring system has weighed data they will never see and declined them, with no loan officer to argue with. Cathy O’Neil calls systems like these “weapons of math destruction” [@oneil2016weapons]: opaque, operating at massive scale, and damaging to the people they score. Decisions that once rested on human judgment are now calculated.
Llull’s Wheels
Thirteenth century theologian Raymond Llull wrote forty treatises on a novel approach to discovering universal truths, collected in his Ars magna [@llull1501ars; see also @gardner1958logic]. The work serves as a user’s manual for a device containing concentric rotating wheels inscribed with letters meant to represent what he believed were the fundamental axioms of truth: God, justice, goodness, eternity, and so on. By turning the wheels, one could explore combinations of these principles and arrive at new metaphysical insights. Llull’s Ars magna stands as one of the earliest documented attempts to apply formal and mechanical reasoning to problems that had previously belonged to philosophy, theology, and human judgment.
Let Us Calculate
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, co-inventor of the calculus and early champion of symbolic logic, encountered Llull’s ideas as a teenager and renamed the method ars combinatoria [@leibniz1666dissertatio]. He expanded Llull’s rotating diagrams into his own interlocking gear mechanisms, which eventually inspired the first mechanical calculator capable of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division: the stepped reckoner. Leibniz imagined a far more ambitious future. He dreamed of a characteristica universalis [@leibniz1981new], a symbolic language that, together with a calculus ratiocinator for reasoning in it, could resolve intellectual disputes through calculation alone. In a later manuscript he wrote [translated in @russell1900critical, p. 170]:

If controversies were to arise, there would be no more need of disputation between two philosophers than between two accountants. For it would suffice to take their pencils in their hands, to sit at their slates, and say to each other (with a friend to witness, if they liked): Let us calculate.

Leibniz’s Dream at Scale
Leibniz believed abstraction and formal symbol manipulation could remove subjective interpretation and lead to universally agreed truths. This vision foreshadows modern computing’s tendency to offload decision making onto mechanical procedures and automated systems. Today we routinely compute outcomes for people at massive scale in the form of mortgage approvals, bail recommendations, algorithmic rankings, and content curation. In a sense Leibniz’s dream has begun to come true, although it invites a difficult question: what do we trade away when we let calculation decide?

blurbs/locke-sicp.title: Locke, Abstraction, and the Programmer’s Toolbox
blurbs/locke-sicp.content:
Chapter 1 of the widely adopted Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs by Abelson, Sussman, and Sussman [-@abelson1996structure] opens with a passage from John Locke’s 1689 Essay Concerning Human Understanding [@locke1689essay], highlighting three fundamental acts of the mind: combining ideas to form more complex ones, identifying relations between them, and abstraction, the act of separating ideas from their particular context to form general concepts:

The acts of the mind, wherein it exerts its power over simple ideas, are chiefly these three: Combining several simple ideas into one compound one, and thus all complex ideas are made. The second is bringing two ideas, whether simple or complex, together, and setting them by one another so as to take a view of them at once, without uniting them into one, by which it gets all its ideas of relations. The third is separating them from all other ideas that accompany them in their real existence: this is called abstraction, and thus all its general ideas are made.

Composition, relation, and abstraction are indeed central to the craft of programming. A skilled programmer recognizes relationships between subproblems, composes solutions into larger structures, and abstracts those solutions into reusable forms. Every successful abstraction becomes a new building block for the next layer of complexity, enabling systems to grow while freeing the developer from rethinking solved details. Composition and relation matter, but abstraction is the engine that lifts everything one level higher.

blurbs/rotman-person-subject-agent.title: Person, Subject, Agent: Rotman's Semiotics and Programming
blurbs/rotman-person-subject-agent.content:
What Semiotics Offers
Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols: how they are constructed, interpreted, and used to convey meaning [@peirce1931collected; @saussure1983course]. Originating in the work of Charles Sanders Peirce and Ferdinand de Saussure, semiotics offers a powerful lens through which to understand programming as a symbolic practice [@tanakaishii2010semiotics]. In software development, programmers do not manipulate reality directly; they manipulate signs that represent data, behaviors, and possibly other symbolic abstracted concepts. As Peirce noted, reasoning about symbols often involves constructing “a sort of skeleton diagram, or outline sketch,” which we then examine to see what holds across cases [@peirce1931collected]. Programming is exactly such a symbolic activity: we create abstract representations, imagine their behavior, and reason about them as stand-ins for real or possible systems.
Semiotic theory is especially relevant to discussions of abstraction, because abstraction involves the transformation into a higher-level symbolic form. When software abstractions are mistaken for the reality they model, or worse, when they displace that reality, we risk losing sight of the ethical and epistemic responsibilities attached to those symbols. Brian Rotman’s semiotics of mathematics helps illuminate how symbolic roles function in both mathematics and programming.
Rotman’s Three Positions
Brian Rotman, in Mathematics as Sign: Writing, Imagining, Counting [-@rotman2000mathematics], develops a semiotic framework inspired by Peirce that helps illuminate the roles involved in symbolic practices such as mathematics and, by extension, programming. Rotman identifies three distinct semiotic positions:

Person: The actual human being who engages with symbolic systems, able to reflect and speak in first-person terms (“I”). The Person navigates contexts, meanings, ethics, and concrete realities.
Subject: A constructed entity defined within the symbolic discourse. In mathematics the Subject is a hypothetical or abstract figure to whom instructions are directed by statements like “let x be a prime number…” or “consider an infinite set”: a typically identityless placeholder within the symbolic system.
Agent: An idealized executor capable of indefinitely performing operations within the symbolic domain as needed (for example, computing potentially infinite sums), embodying automation or algorithmic execution without consciousness or reflective awareness, not even that of the imagined Subject one level above.

Mapping onto Programming
When mapped onto software development, these three roles align with familiar concepts:

The Person corresponds to the programmer, capable of reasoning consciously, ethically, and contextually.
The Subject aligns with abstract computational models (a conceptual machine or an abstract data structure): entities defined symbolically by the programmer but not actualized as tangible hardware, which the programmer instructs through a programming language.
The Agent corresponds to the computer hardware or CPU, tirelessly executing symbolic instructions without reflection or awareness.


























Semiotic actorMathematicsProgrammingPersonThe mathematician engaging with symbolic systems, reflecting consciously, ethically, and contextually.The programmer, consciously reflecting on the ethical implications and real-world contexts of code.SubjectAbstract entities, the subject of symbolic discourse (“let x be…”), existing only symbolically.Computational models or symbolic structures: theoretical machines, data structures, algorithms defined by the programmer.AgentIdealized executor performing indefinite symbolic manipulations automatically, without reflection or awareness.Computer hardware or CPU, executing instructions automatically and mechanically without conscious reflection or ethical awareness.
Rotman’s semiotic trichotomy of mathematics, projected onto programming, reveals how abstractionism collapses crucial distinctions among these roles, privileging abstract Subjects and mechanical Agents at the direction of a Person who is sometimes reflective and sometimes not. Software abstractions thus risk becoming disconnected from human understanding and ethical responsibility precisely when the symbolic system replaces reflective human judgment with automated, unreflective execution.
Keeping the Person in View
What Rotman’s scheme offers is a name for each role, including the one that is easiest to forget. Every program is written by a Person, addressed to a Subject, and carried out by an Agent, and only the first of these can ask what the program is for. Abstraction makes it easy to spend the whole day talking to the Subject while the Agent does the work. The question worth keeping in view is where the Person went.

blurbs/simondon.title: Thinking About Software, Programming, and AI with Simondon
blurbs/simondon.content:
In the early 1900s, starting a car took skill and a little courage. The driver set the choke and adjusted the spark timing by hand, walked around to the front of the car, and heaved on a crank; if the engine fired at the wrong moment, the crank could kick back hard enough to break a wrist. In 1912 Cadillac introduced Charles Kettering’s electric starter, and the crank gave way to a switch, and later to a key turned in the ignition. Today many cars start with a single button that hides a whole sequence of events: the car confirms that the key fob is inside, exchanges a coded handshake with it to unlock the immobiliser, checks that your foot is on the brake, primes the fuel pump, and only then turns the engine over. At every step the driver has needed to know less about engines, and more people have been able to drive.
Simondon on opacity and ubiquity of technology
Gilbert Simondon observed [-@simondon2017mode] that technologies tend to become more socially integrated as they grow less internally intelligible to their users. As devices evolve, their functions fold into self-regulating, interdependent systems that no longer require interpretive knowledge to operate. This process, that Simondon calls concretization, produces machines that work reliably and autonomously while concealing their inner logic. Opacity, rather than hindering adoption, is what allows technologies to become ubiquitous; they turn ordinary once they stop being complicated objects of inquiry and start working quietly in the background. Heidegger proposed similar interpretations of technology use.
Applying the idea to programming
Though Simondon was writing about machines rather than code, a similar pattern appears in programming, where abstraction separates interface from implementation. As code becomes more complex and layered, users of a programming abstraction, whether a function, module, or API, need only understand how to interact with its surface, not its internal machinery. Integration and encapsulation make a system more capable and, at the same time, more opaque! The most widely used software tools, from operating systems to machine-learning libraries, thrive on this asymmetry: they are trusted for their results rather than their mechanisms. In both technics and code, ubiquity grows in step with invisibility, as abstraction becomes the price and the precondition of shared collective use.
A tension with explainable AI
This dynamic sets up an obvious tension in the age of LLM-generated code, text, and images. The same forces that drive the spread of AI (automation, integration, and ease of use) also make its inner workings opaque to most users. Large models become ubiquitous precisely because they function like Simondon’s concretized machines: reliable, efficient, and inscrutable. Yet the push for explainable AI demands the opposite: transparency, interpretability, and human understanding. The challenge is that the qualities that make AI widely usable are the very ones that create barriers to explanation.
An observation on terminology
Interestingly, there seems to be a conflict of terminology. Simondon names concretization as the process whereby machines and other technologies become more opaque, and thereby more reliable, while increasing in simplicity of use. Meanwhile, most computer scientists would refer to the analogous process in programming as abstraction, while concretization is the opposite of abstraction.

blurbs/symbolic-reasoning-math-logic-cs.title: Meaningless Symbols in Twentieth Century Symbolic Reasoning
blurbs/symbolic-reasoning-math-logic-cs.content:
Hilbert, Gödel, and the Rise of Formalism
A crucial turning point in the history of formal reasoning occurred in 1900, when David Hilbert challenged the world’s leading mathematicians to show that all mathematical truths could be confirmed through formal proof [@hilbert1902mathematical]. This project ignited an intense focus on grounding mathematics in logic and set theory, until results by Gödel, Turing, Church, and others revealed fundamental limits on formal provability [@smullyan1992godel; @turing1936computable; @church1936unsolvable]. Within this climate of ambition, Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead produced their monumental Principia Mathematica [-@whitehead1927principia], a purely symbolic treatment of arithmetic intended to demonstrate that rigorous manipulation of formal notation could serve as the foundation of mathematical truth.
Whitehead, reflecting on years of labor devoted to symbolic representation, articulated an influential defense of abstraction in An Introduction to Mathematics [-@whitehead1911introduction]:

By relieving the brain of all unnecessary work, a good notation sets it free to concentrate on more advanced problems and, in effect, increases the mental power of the race […] It is a profoundly erroneous truism […] that we should cultivate the habit of thinking of what we are doing. The precise opposite is the case. Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations we can perform without thinking about them.

Whitehead draws attention to the power of symbol manipulation separated from semantic content. Progress, in his view, depends on freeing thought from the burden of details so that higher level reasoning can flourish. This is perhaps the clearest declaration of the abstractionist ethos in the entire historical record. Similar values persist in contemporary design culture, echoed in Steve Krug’s Don’t Make Me Think [-@krug2013dont]. While abstraction allows us to manage complexity, we encourage modern software engineers to think critically about the decisions that abstraction quietly hides.
Abstraction in Computing
Edsger Dijkstra later expressed a related ideal, celebrating the manipulation of symbols without regard for their meaning [-@dijkstra2002ewd1300]:

I must mention our desire to let the symbols do the work, more precisely: as much of the work as profitably possible. The formalist prefers to manipulate his formulae, temporarily ignoring all interpretations they might admit; the rules for the permissible symbol manipulations being formulated in terms of those symbols. The formalist calculates with uninterpreted formulae.

Claude Shannon took a similar position in the early foundations of information theory [-@shannon1948mathematical]:

The fundamental problem of communication is that of reproducing at one point either exactly or approximately a message selected at another point. Frequently the messages have meaning; that is, they refer to or are correlated according to some system with certain physical or conceptual entities. These semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem.

Nathaniel Borenstein later satirized abstractionist tendencies in software engineering [-@borenstein1991programming]:

It should be noted that no ethically trained software engineer would ever consent to write a DestroyBaghdad procedure. Basic professional ethics would instead require him to write a DestroyCity procedure, to which Baghdad could be given as a parameter.

This short historical tour illustrates that abstractionism has shaped computational thinking long before the formal birth of computer science. The question we inherit is how to balance the power of forgetting details with the moral and practical responsibilities that abstraction obscures.

concepts/abstraction-leak.title: Abstraction leak
concepts/abstraction-leak.content:
An abstraction leaks when details it was meant to hide break through its surface: the network timeout behind a “simple” file read, the spinning wheel behind a word processor. Joel Spolsky’s “law of leaky abstractions” [-@spolsky2002law] says every non-trivial abstraction does this to some degree. A leak is the programmer’s version of Heidegger’s broken hammer: the tool suddenly becomes an object.
Discussed in

Heidegger and Software

concepts/abstraction.title: Abstraction
concepts/abstraction.content:
Abstraction is the act of keeping some distinctions and deliberately dropping others, so that many particular things can be handled as one general thing. Locke called it separating ideas “from all other ideas that accompany them in their real existence”; programmers do the same when they write a function, an interface, or a type. Every abstraction is therefore also a decision about what to forget.

concepts/characteristica-universalis.title: Characteristica universalis
concepts/characteristica-universalis.content:
Leibniz’s imagined universal symbolic language, in which every concept would have a precise sign. Paired with a calculus ratiocinator for reasoning in that language, it would let disputes be settled by calculation: “Let us calculate.” It anticipates formal logic, programming languages, and the hope that judgment can be computed.
Discussed in

Early Mechanical Reasoning and the Dream of Universal Calculation

concepts/concretization.title: Concretization
concepts/concretization.content:
For Gilbert Simondon, concretization is the process by which a technical object’s parts come to depend on and support one another, until the machine becomes a coherent, self-regulating whole. Concretized machines are more reliable and easier to use, and harder to understand from the outside. Computer scientists would call the analogous process abstraction, and use “concretization” for its opposite.
Discussed in

Thinking About Software, Programming, and AI with Simondon

concepts/ready-to-hand.title: Ready-to-hand
concepts/ready-to-hand.content:
Heidegger’s term (zuhanden) for equipment that has withdrawn into use: the hammer you are hammering with, the keyboard you are typing on. When the tool breaks or fails, it becomes present-at-hand (vorhanden), an object to be noticed and inspected. Most good abstractions aim to stay ready-to-hand.
Discussed in

Heidegger and Software

concepts/syllogism.title: Syllogism
concepts/syllogism.content:
Aristotle’s form of deductive argument: two premises sharing a middle term yield a conclusion. All Xs are Y; Z is an X; therefore Z is Y. Its validity depends only on form, not on what X, Y, and Z mean. That is both its power and, as the penguin shows, its blind spot.
Discussed in

Formal Methods in Ancient Greece

index.title: XBSTRXCT
index.content:
XBSTRXCT is a growing collection of micro-essays (and occasional full-sized essays) related to the concept of abstraction. The posts tend to blend programming, computation, mathematics, and philosophy.
A note before you read: these essays are my attempt to work through ideas as I learn them, not the last word on any of them. Some of what’s here is surely incomplete or wrong. If you spot a mistake, I’d be glad to hear about it.
Abstraction
From Latin abstractio, from the verb abstrahere, “to draw away”.

thinking in terms of ideas rather than particular things.
in art, freedom from depicting things as they appear.
considering something apart from its circumstances, attributes, or concrete companions.
